10864-a-visit-to-the-monastery-of-la-tra:
W. D. Fellowes published A Visit to the Monastery of La Trappe in 1817. Its notes come from a tour through Le Perche, Normandy, Bretagne, Poitou, Anjou, the Bocage, Touraine, Orleans, and the environs of Paris. Colored engravings from drawings made on the spot show the monastery, ruined churches, the grotto of Heloise at Clisson, and tombs of Abelard and Heloise.

Fellowes disavows high literary pretension, offering plain notes of places, monks, and ruins. His tour mixes devotion, antiquarian curiosity, and scenery. Readers get a Regency travel book, rich in pictures of western France after the wars.
12163-the-sleeper-awakes-a-revised-editi:
H. G. Wells revised his 1899 novel When the Sleeper Wakes as The Sleeper Awakes, the version printed here. It is early science fiction, set in London more than two centuries after its hero falls into a trance.

Graham, an insomniac, wakes to find his modest savings have grown, through compound interest, into ownership of half the world. A Council rules in his name while the city has become a vast machine of moving walkways, roof gardens, and crowded under-city labor. Drawn into revolt against the Council, Graham must choose between the rulers who kept him asleep and the people who claim to free him. The novel asks who truly owns a future built on inherited wealth.
16041-the-grey-cloak:
A historical romance by Harold MacGrath, author of The Puppet Crown, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1903. Thomas Mitchell Peirce supplied the pictures. MacGrath dedicates the book to his cousin Lillian A. Baldwin, who, like Stevenson, loves a story for the story's sake. The grey cloak itself gives the tale its mystery.

A man in the cloak, the toilet of the chevalier, and a mutilated something open the chapters, in MacGrath's brisk manner. Swords, love, and intrigue follow through old France. MacGrath writes for readers who liked dash and romance. The novel delights as a cloak-and-sword tale: a hero in grey, a lady in peril, and adventure at every turn.
20985-the-banner-boy-scouts-on-a-tour-or:
Old favourites parade again in The Banner Boy Scouts on a Tour, George A. Warren promises. New faces join the troop for the mystery of Rattlesnake Mountain in this 1912 tale. The book stands alone yet forms the set's second link, Warren notes.

Scout hikes, camp craft, and a mountain mystery drive the boys' tour. Warren wrote when scouting was new and its tales sold fast and wide. Codes, knots, signals, and woodcraft season the adventure throughout. Readers get a clear taste of how the Boy Scouts gripped American boys, in fiction built to preach scout law by deed.
27568-sketches-of-our-life-at-sarawak:
Harriette McDougall wrote these sketches of life at Sarawak, published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge in London, with a New York edition from E. and J. B. Young. A map accompanies the volume, and a frontispiece shows a man felling a reptile with a stout walking-stick.

McDougall had published Letters from Sarawak, addressed to a Child, nearly thirty years before, and she extends the story here over twenty years. Chapters cover the court-house, College Hill, pirates, the church and school, the girls, and a boat journey to the Rejang. Chinese insurrection, a Malay plot, and a Malay wedding follow. The sketches give a missionary family's Borneo life.
30002-sjambak:
Jack Vance wrote Sjambak, with pictures by Virgil Finlay. Its headnote says Wilbur Murphy sought romance, excitement, and an impossible Horseman of Space. The planet frustrated him with polite smiles at every turn, until he found them all the hard way. The tale opens at Know Your Universe, a show whose production director, Howard Frayberg, calls the program dull and stuck in a rut.

Continuity editor Sam Catlin agrees in part. Seaweed Processors of Alphard IX draws no one. Next week brings the Ball Expedition to the Mixtup Mountains on Gropus. Frayberg wants a new slant, with glamor, mystery, and thrills, and the old human angle. Catlin pulls a smoothed-out page from his waste basket: Murphy's idea to investigate the Horseman of Space, the man who rides up to meet incoming spaceships. Vance keeps the satire brisk and the wonder close.
32212-clean-break:
Roger Dee's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1953, follows a veterinarian who gave up a wilder dream.  Its tagline notes that a veteran veterinarian might have fled, but Watts had to help any sick animal. Oliver Watts's life held nothing more exciting than being turned down by his draft board over a punctured eardrum. Deferring to his Aunt Katisha and his elder sister Glenna, he took up veterinary medicine at twenty-five.

Oliver's relinquished dream, cherished since childhood, was to become a hunter and trainer of jungle animals. Aunt Katisha discouraged it firmly, maintaining that the last male Watts must not risk his skin in so perilous a pursuit, and she won. Readers get a gentle science-fiction character story, where duty to family, duty to animals, and a lost jungle dream pull one man in different directions.
33839-problem-on-balak:
Roger Dee writes a science-fiction novelette in this Galaxy story from September 1953, illustrated by Dick Francis. A four-person field team from Solar Exploitations discovers Balak, a small planet circling 70 Ophiuchi some 20,000 light-years from Earth. There it finds the galaxy's greatest race of surgeons, masters of structural and neural work. The Balakians hand the visitors a life-and-death problem.

Captain Corelli, Gibbons, and the narrator meet their first Balakian native barely a hundred yards from the ship S. E. 2100. They collect soil and vegetation samples with a wary eye for predators. Dee's tale turns on an unexpected solution to an apparently impossible medical dilemma. Readers of classic pulp science fiction will enjoy its brisk narration, alien medicine, and ironic twist.
5959-peveril-of-the-peak:
Walter Scott begins far back, with William Peveril riding beside William the Conqueror to Hastings. The Norman king rewards his namesake with lands and lordships in Derbyshire, and the new baron raises a Gothic fortress above the mouth of the Devil's Cavern. That stronghold gives Castleton its name.

From this feudal root the narrative moves toward civil strife, when foul words, jealousies, and fears set folk together by the ears. Scott uses the Peveril line to tie a family seat to wider English quarrels. The opening sets place, blood, and old stone firmly before the plot quickens.
8435-the-sturdy-oak:
Fourteen American authors wrote this composite novel of American politics, chapter by chapter, with Samuel Merwin first among them. Harry Leon Wilson, Fannie Hurst, Dorothy Canfield, and Kathleen Norris each take a hand. Henry Kitchell Webster, Anne O'Hagan, Mary Heaton Vorse, and Alice Duer Miller join them, with Ethel Watts Mumford, Marjorie Benton Cooke, William Allen White, and others.

The sturdy oak of the title stands for American political life, and the novel follows its characters through campaigns, ideals, and compromises, each author carrying the story forward in turn. Readers get a curiosity and a panorama: many voices, one plot, and a picture of how leading writers of the day saw politics. The seams show, and that is part of the fun.
9393-a-dish-of-orts-chiefly-papers-on-th:
George MacDonald called this book A Dish of Orts, or scraps, chiefly papers on imagination and Shakespeare. In his preface he doubts the title, lest readers think he offers worthless bits. No man, he says, would insult readers with valueless scraps. These papers, even two caught from spoken words, cost no trifling labor.

They are fragmentary presentments of larger meditation, his friends may take them as such. Topics range from fancy to the Bard, in MacDonald's searching voice. The book remains a rich sampler of his thought, best dipped into slowly, piece by piece.
9856-the-inn-at-the-red-oak:
Latta Griswold's 1917 novel opens at a country inn where an old French marquis arrives, bringing memories of exile and revolution. His nights at the inn, the oak parlor, and walks through the woods set a quiet, haunted mood.

A torn scrap of paper, a disappearance, and strange green lights turn the story toward mystery, with recollections of a French exile at its heart. Griswold blends romance and suspense in an old-house setting. Readers who like gentle ghostly tales with a French flavor will enjoy its atmosphere and its patient, old-fashioned charm.
9974-the-yellow-streak:
Valentine Williams's mystery opens at Harkings, the house of Hartley Parrish, a man newly risen to wealth. His greatest pride is Bude, his large, comfortable butler, and the early chapters move through twilight discoveries, a letter, and voices in the library.

Robin Greve, Mary, and the puzzling Mr. Manderton enter the tangle, with clues mounting toward a code king, a man with a yellow face, and the reading of a riddle. Williams keeps the country-house puzzle turning. Readers get a classic mystery where the title's yellow streak marks fear, guilt, or both.
a-dish-of-orts-chiefly-papers-on-the-ima: George MacDonald gathers papers on the imagination and on Shakespeare in a dish of orts. Its essays treat the functions and culture of imagination, individual development, and the art of Shakespeare as revealed by himself. Other pieces discuss the elder Hamlet, polish, and Browning's Christmas Eve. MacDonald writes with earnest thought about art, faith, and the mind.
a-visit-to-the-monastery-of-la-trappe-in: William Dorset Fellowes visits the monastery of La Trappe in 1817. His notes come from a tour through Le Perche, Normandy, Bretagne, Poitou, Anjou, Le Bocage, Touraine, Orleanois, and the environs of Paris. Coloured engravings from drawings made on the spot show the monastery and ruins of its ancient church and gateway. The grotto of Heloise at Clisson and the tomb of Abelard and Heloise appear among the plates. The preface disavows any higher pretension than simple notes.
britannica-1911-adam-s-peak:
Adam's Peak is a mountain in Ceylon. It stands about forty-five miles east of Colombo. The peak rises steeply to over seven thousand feet. A magnificent prospect rewards the climb. Its conical summit ends in an oblong platform. A hollow there resembles a human foot. The hollow measures over five feet long. Sinhalese Buddhists consecrate it as Buddha's footprint. Gems ornament the margin of the impression. A wooden canopy protects it from weather.

Three faiths claim the one footprint. A resident priest receives pilgrims' offerings there. He blesses them before their departure down. Muslims regard the print as Adam's own. Adam did a thousand years' penance there, they say. Hindus claim the footprint for their god Siva.
britannica-1911-aimak:
Aimak, or Eimak, names certain tribes of Afghanistan, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is Mongolian for a clan, or section of a tribe. The Aimak are nomadic or partly settled peoples of Mongolian stock. They live in the highlands north and northwest of Herat, and number upwards of a quarter of a million.

Originally they were known as the four Eimaks, from their four main tribes. The Taimani predominate in Ghur, alongside the Ferozkhoi and the Jamshidi, with the Hazara counted by some authorities. Aimak speech is said to be close to Kalmuck. They are Sunni Muslims, unlike the Shia Hazara, and mostly of Iranian or near-Iranian blood where the Hazara are Turanian. The entry calls them a bold, wild people and renowned fighters.
britannica-1911-arawak:
Arawak is a tribe of South American Indians. They live in Dutch and British Guiana. Their name means meal-eaters, probably. Cassava was their staple food. The tribe gave its name to a linguistic stock. That stock, Arawakan, includes many tribes. Some member tribes were once powerful. Their range was once enormous geographically. It stretched from southern Brazil to Central America.

The whole West Indies were occupied once. Settlements even reached Florida's seaboard. Spaniards found Arawaks in Haiti especially. Caribs had expelled them from most islands. The Arawaks proper were undersized and peaceable. Agriculture was their way of life. They were Guiana's most civilised people. Their weaving skills were notable. Stone and gold work also distinguished them. Im Thurn's Guiana study anchors the references.
britannica-1911-barley-break:
Barley-break is an old English country game, often mentioned by poets of the 17th and 18th centuries. Three pairs played it, each pair a man and a woman, stationed in three bases or plots that touched one another. The game turns on chase and escape within that small ground.

The couple in the middle base, called hell or prison, tried to catch the other two pairs. A chased player might break, darting aside, to avoid capture. If one of a pair was caught, both were condemned to hell and took the middle place. From the game, the 1911 Britannica entry explains, came the phrase the last couple in hell, often heard in old plays.
britannica-1911-bleak: Bleak, also called blick, is a small river fish of the carp family, named Alburnus lucidus in the entry. It is kin to the bream and the minnow, but longer in the body, like a sardine. It lives in streams across Europe. Anglers catch it, and it is kept in aquariums. The entry turns last to trade. Its scales hold a shiny colouring matter. In France and Germany that matter fed a large trade in false pearls. The hosted text breaks off mid-point.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-mrak:
Ignatius Mrak was the second bishop of Marquette in the United States, born in 1818 at Hotovle in the diocese of Laibach, Austria, and dead at Marquette in 1901. He studied classics at Laibach and theology in its diocesan seminary, and was ordained in 1837. To qualify as tutor to Field-Marshal Baron Pirquet's household, he passed a rigorous state examination and spent two years at Legnago near Verona.

Returning to his diocese in 1840, he served as assistant before emigrating to America five years later. Detroit's Bishop Lefebre sent him at once to Arbre Croche to assist the famed Indian missionary Francis Pierz. They worked fruitfully together for two years, and when Pierz moved to Minnesota in 1851, Mrak kept the Indian mission. Baraga made him vicar-general, and on Baraga's death he became Marquette's second bishop, long refusing to accept the honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincenz-hasak:
Vincenz Hasak was a Bohemian historian and collector who lived from 1812 to 1889. Born at Neustadt near Friedland, he studied classics and theology at Leitmeritz, served eighteen years as chaplain at Arnsdorf, then until death as pastor at Weisskirchlitz, where he died as dean. While chaplain he began collecting old books, paintings, engravings, gems, and shells, building a small but valuable museum that astonished connoisseurs.

A library famed above all for rare early printed books, including ten pre-Reformation German Bible translations. He put his treasures to scientific use in books on medieval German religious life and language, notably a study of the German people's Christian faith at the Middle Ages' close. Treating ninety-three printed books and manuscripts, and a documentary account of Luther and the religious literature of his time to 1520.
doe-osti-3012982-characterizing-the-impa: Water uptake got absorption-characterized, and this DOE text studies aerosol particles. The pages detail the light findings. The atmospheric folks get their data. The uptake was water. The data were atmospheric. The particles were aerosol. The absorption was light.
peveril-of-the-peak:
Walter Scott's Peveril of the Peak opens with a long pedigree. William Peveril, supposed son of the Conqueror, built his fortress over the Devil's Cavern at Castleton in Derbyshire, choosing his nest as an eagle chooses an eyry. His descendants kept the proud title of Peverils of the Peak long after the great fief was forfeited.

In Charles the Second's time the family head is Sir Geoffrey Peveril, proud, lavish, convivial, and ruled by prejudice. Scott sets this old Cavalier house against its Puritan neighbours. The novel that follows, of the Popish Plot years, grows from the feud between the two households.
podcast-dannyjones-XE8h7EuUrAk:
Norman Ohler joins Danny Jones to talk about drug use in Nazi Germany, the subject of his best known book. The episode title points at Adolf Hitler's own drug habits. Ohler is a writer who dug through German archives and medical files for his research.

Ohler explains how meth and other drugs spread through the German army and the public. He also covers the drugs given to Hitler by his own doctor. Jones draws out the parts of the war that this drug use may help explain. Listeners get a strange but well sourced side of the Third Reich that school history tends to skip.
podcast-dannyjones-xLOGdyv0_Ak:
Biologist Bret Weinstein brings a dark warning to the Danny Jones podcast: some actors, he says, want to bring about the apocalypse. The episode ties that claim to the Epstein case and to the risk of war with Iran. Weinstein is known for grim readings of elite behavior.

Weinstein lays out why he thinks certain leaders and networks court chaos rather than fear it. He connects Epstein's protected status to a deeper rot in Western institutions. Jones pushes him on evidence and on what can be done. The wary and watchful get a tense, serious talk about power at its worst.
podcast-joerogan--btTC-bepAk:
Teacher Sadhguru joins Joe Rogan to talk about the lost sense of heaven in a segment from the show. Sadhguru is an Indian yogi with a vast crowd of fans across the world. His talks mix jokes with deep claims on the soul.

Sadhguru tells how the old sense of heaven as a real aim of life has thinned in the West. He argues men now chase goods and miss the bliss at hand. Rogan asks what a man should seek in its place. Listeners get a wise, warm cut. The library holds the segment as an archive record of his teaching as stated.
podcast-tuckercarlson-AMBCkokxTAk:
Brigham Buhler works in health care finance and advocacy, and he joins Tucker Carlson after the assassination of UnitedHealthcare's chief executive shocked the insurance industry. Their subject is the business underneath that killing: what Buhler describes as the mass monetization of chronic illness in American medicine.

Buhler argues the system earns more from managed sickness than from cures, and he names the incentives that keep patients on lifelong treatment. Carlson connects the account to public anger at insurers, which the killing exposed in an ugly form. The episode neither celebrates the murder nor treats it as meaningless; it uses the moment to prosecute an industry. Listeners get an insider's version of why American health care costs what it costs.
the-grey-cloak: Harold MacGrath wrote The Grey Cloak. MacGrath is named as author of The Puppet Crown. Thomas Mitchell Peirce made the pictures. Grosset and Dunlap published the book in New York in 1903. It is dedicated to the author's cousin, Lillian A. Baldwin. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication, and the start of a contents list. The first heads are The Man in the Cloak and The Toilet of the Chevalier. No chapter text is present.
the-inn-at-the-red-oak: Latta Griswold published this novel in 1917. A frontispiece shows a boy named Dan crying out. The thing before him is a treasure, he says. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The contents divide the book into three parts. The Old Marquis comes first. The Torn Scrap of Paper follows. The Schooner in the Cove closes it. Headings promise a lion's eye jewel. Green lights and a French exile's memories appear. Midnight vigils and a Madame de la Fontaine follow.
the-little-lame-prince-and-his-travellin: The Little Lame Prince and His Travelling Cloak, by Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, appears here in a Rand-McNally edition carrying a 1909 copyright and marked as the edition of 1937. Only the transcriber's note, copyright page, and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list eight chapters with page numbers, covering the single title tale. That sets this record apart from the companion record of The Little Lame Prince, whose contents add five extra tales after the main story.
the-sleeper-awakes-a-revised-edition-of-: H. G. Wells's The Sleeper Awakes is billed as a revised edition of When the Sleeper Wakes. The date 1899 appears under his name. The pages shown give a contents list of twenty chapters and no story text. Insomnia opens the list, then the trance and the awakening. The moving ways and the hall of the Atlas follow. The people march at chapter nine, with a battle of the darkness next. Ostrog is introduced at chapter twelve. The monoplane, Graham remembers, and Ostrog's point of view come later.
the-sturdy-oak:
Elizabeth Jordan collected this composite novel of American politics. She edited it very cautiously, as she says. Fourteen American authors wrote it on a theme by Mary Austin. Henry Holt published it in 1917. The named contributors include Samuel Merwin, Harry Leon Wilson, Fannie Hurst, Dorothy Canfield, Kathleen Norris, Alice Duer Miller, William Allen White, and Mary Austin herself.

Jordan's preface explains that a committee meeting in the spring of 1916 agreed to ask fourteen leading authors, known to be generous as well as gifted, for a chapter each. Jordan was absent from that meeting. The others joyously assigned her the trivial details. She had to get the novel together. She began by persuading each busy author to write. The joke frames the whole experiment in joint fiction.
the-yellow-streak: Valentine Williams's The Yellow Streak is represented here by a contents list of twenty-eight chapters and a chapter heading. Robin Greve and Mr. Manderton figure in several titles. A silent shot and a sheet of blue paper promise mystery. The death of Hartley Parrish closes the list. Chapter one, The Master of Harkings, is announced but its text stops there. Nothing more of the story appears in the pages present.
